author: Papa
content: You need to get over FEAR and GREED!  Don't trade more than 2 times in a day period is a staring point.  Take the profit at the stop every time period.  Develop consistency in these first two aspects and don't chase trades.  These things helped me a lot.  There is always another day to trade.  What Tony and Jack have really shown is patience, that goes a long way and I appreciate seeing that in the past week.

author: Papa
content: I would also recommend that you make notes on your charts, entry and exits.  What did you see and why you entered and exited, did you add and chase etc.  Since you have TOS it's rather easy to do this, take a screenshot and look at this closely, you'll really discover your habits and if they are consistent then you have great hope of fixing them.  Basically you are doing a post mortem analysis of yourself.

author: Torr
content:
The way I've managed this is two loses, I scale down for the day to half risk on everything. If I lose three in a row, I'm done. I only risk .5 R ever, so I only need 1.5 trades to go right to be back to green the next day. If I have a string of losing days (two in a row), I scale down at the start of the next day. Two green days, and I scale up again. My reasoning for this is that I'm losing either because 1. I don't have the edge I think I do (perhaps because market conditions have shifted without me knowing) 2. My head isn't right 3. I'm just hitting a losing streak, which is probalistic certainty in trading. Either of these options mean it's better to just scale back or stop. 

But I also get it that we get hijacked sometimes.

author: Jdub
content: No one knows the exact amount that the  contracts will be worth at a certain price due to the greeks always moving. The reason I said 14 was my risk is becasue if you see on the options contract that was the break of strucutre level. If price closed below the key level the contracts would be worth around 14 ish. In this case it was an a+ setup. I usually risk around $2000 on A+ setups. Lets say I wanted to risk $3500 on a trade where the contracts are worth $1.75 then my stop would be at $1.40 on the contracts.

author: Jdub
content: Yes. When trading options espically right off of the open it can be hard to manage risk sometimes becuase price moves so quick. The easiest way is to look at the options chart real quick to give you an idea of how much your risking. If price is consolidating and you have more time you can calculate the risk amount with delta for a more precise risk amount. That's why when you risk a same amount per trade you understand lets say for example tsla I only need to give it 10% to know if I'm right or wrong. So if I usually risk 10% that means I will risk $750-$1000. That means my posistion size will be anywhere between $7500-10,000 position size depedning on the price of the contracts.

author: BackwoodsDisco
content:
I made a google spreadsheet that calculates it all, based on account size and how much I want to risk each trade. Once I used it for a while, I got the general idea and do quick math in my head
Say you have 20k and you want to risk 3% on each trade. That’s $600 risk per trade. If you set a 10% stop loss, then total contract value would be $6000. So, $6000 divided by the cost of each contract = how many contracts to buy.

content: if anyone can learn anything please learn from me. I took 175.18 retest on tesla, only 2 contracts (normal size is 4 contracts) Scaled 1 at HOD 176, held the last one into previous high and instead of selling out of my position which would have been a $200 day for me it ended break even and only $65. Oversized and took 10 contracts of the apple trade, that failed and put me down $200 on the day instead. If you have one good trade PLEASE walk away from the screens . I shouldve been happy with the trade on tesla and instead i was focused on the dollar amount and in the long run it didnt end well.

author: 👑 of Puts
content: I'd like to share few things. It's been 2 months in this room. And i had my attention glued to mainly learning. Taken probably about 10-15 trades in 2 months😵‍💫  Could have really followed the call outs and made money  🤌  But i can't take something i don't understand. Here's a few things that really helped: Creating a proper playbook with screenshots and entry/exit criteria; Backtesting each setup (proper backtesting, i realized i did it wrong all those years); doing video trade reviews (same as Tony and Jake do on youtube. created a channel and posting it there) Helps so much! Also created a discord where i post my watchlist and my thoughts. Having my thoughts written out helps with discipline!!! Some days i think i didn't make any progress so i made a list of things i learned in 2 months and it's impressive. Next step is getting off the lives and doing my own stream so i can talk through my thoughts and watch my emotions. Will review posted lives for my mistakes and thought process. I really need to hear my own thoughts otherwise i'm distracted. Some people can do 3 things at once, but it's not me. My main message here i guess i can't do less than Tony or Jake and be profitable.

Hi Gaby. It's never about account size, but about how much work you put in.
It's a different path for everyone, the emotions involved at the time of taking decisions on a Trade kick in differently.

author: EY
content:
CPI summarized : Here's a simple summary of the important points from the Consumer Price Index report for June 2024:

1. **Prices Went Down a Little**: Overall, prices of things went down a tiny bit in June. Before June, they didn't change in May.
  
2. **Gasoline Prices**: The price for gasoline (what cars use to run) went down a lot in June after going down a bit in May.

3. **Energy Prices**: Things like electricity and gas for heating homes also got a bit cheaper in June, just like in May.

4. **Food Prices**: The price of food you buy to eat at home went up a tiny bit in June. The price of food you eat out (like in restaurants) went up a bit more.

5. **Other Items**: For things that aren't food or energy, prices went up a tiny bit in June.

6. **12-Month Summary**: Over the past year, overall prices went up by 3.0%, which is a bit less than they went up in the previous 12 months.

So, some prices went down, some went up a little, but overall, prices didn't change much in June compared to before. Over the last year, things cost more than they did the year before.

author: TonyMontana
content:
Just read all this, as it got brought up to my attention.

A couple things, in terms of stats I’ve had 8 losing days in the last almost 2 months.

All trades taken on voice or text live, not hindsight.

In terms of this market, yes it’s a lil choppy, however I literally could not emphasize that point more in trade reviews daily.


If you think you’re consistently going to make a lot of money trading every market, it’s wrong.

You have ups and downs no matter how long you have been trading, that’s just how market cycles are.

It’s being able to know when to control your risk and when to push your risk you make the most money.

As a trader stop predicting moves, your main role is to be a risk manager.

Finally, if you’re here for signals over education, then that also isn’t going to help you in the long run.


I know our stats, you can join any discord it won’t even come close.

Patience is key to long term trading.

Hey everyone,

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
content:
I completely agree! 
I’ve noticed that most losses among my peers often come from a lack of patience. One of the things I love about the Break and Retest strategy is that it gives us the chance to WAIT for Price Action to react to key levels. But sometimes, we get ahead of ourselves and pull the trigger as soon as the price touches a level.

The risk here is that, since we’re waiting for a pullback, the price might move even further before reversing. So, remember, this strategy really rewards PATIENCE. Keep that in mind and maybe even write it down and stick it near your screen as a reminder.

author: Aleksandra Seliverstova
content:
Hi guys, this might be interesting to anyone struggling with RR like I do. I revised my trades (made during live sessions) of the last month, and here's the stats.

There were 10 losing trades (exit on SL, actually 9, but for one trade I couldn't remember the setup so I counted it as a loss in terms of this analysis), and 12 winning trades. 3 of the losses were on FOMC day, so they can actually be excluded as I shouldn't have taken them at all. But still.

RR of the winning trades: 
9,39
4,73
4,07
2,08
3,29
2,05
4,32
3,04
1,4
3,16
5,18
3,3
That's if I didn't close position until the initial stop loss was hit and just waited until the trend changes or the day ends, and took profit at maximum (which you never know for sure, of course).

So there was only one trade with RR less than 2.
I'm actually red this month due to uneven risk management and selling 30-50% of the position at HoD most of the times (I trade 4-6 cons).

So I made these calculations to understand what kind of result I would have now if I only sold at 2RR or 3RR.
Check the screenshot, it's all there. 
If you trade a small number of cons as I do you might come to the same conclusion as I did, that even closing the whole position at 3RR without taking partial scales at HoD/LoD might have been rather profitable.

Of course, that's a random month and these stats aren't really representative. But I personally want to try something like selling 4 cons out of 6 at 2RR, and the rest (2) at 3RR.

Hope this is helpful 🙌

author: Aleksandra Seliverstova
content:
I never moved my SL to BE, I just scaled out 30-50% at HoD/LoD and scaled out the rest at psychological numbers and final target without any trailers. This led me to playing most of the time at RR 1:1, if not worse. That's why I decided to check the actual potential RR of the trades I took.

As for the analysis, you can see above that of my 9 losing trades I could restore, only 1 could use scaling out at HoD/LoD, and the rest of losing trades never reached HoD/LoD. So, if of my 12 winning trades I scale all of them 50% at HoD/LoD, that's 50% loss of potential profit of 12 trades, compared to this one trade where kinda saved 1/2 of risk by scaling out at HoD/LoD.

Of my trades of this month, many times price was kinda consolidating right after the entry, so closing position at BE didn't make any sense most of the time

Like this trade on AAPL I took on August 19th. Most of the time it's like this. The price is indecisive and then it breaks up or down. If I cut the position at BE, considering the entry price, the RR just doesn't make sense.

author: BullBearXInsights
content:
I’ve been part of several trading groups, and every time I joined one, I ended up blowing my account. When I traded on my own, I managed to make some profits. After joining this group, I blew my account again, and I realized it was because of me. I lacked focus and started relying too much on others' decisions instead of my own. I forgot that my purpose for joining the group was to learn from their trading mindset—how they think and trade. Believe me, Tony and Jack are the best compared to other groups out there.

One key lesson I learned was to do my homework, compare my analysis with theirs, and make decisions based on my own playbook. I started trading with smaller sizes, learning how they form their opinions. Interestingly, while I’m now closely aligned with their views, I still make slightly different decisions when it comes to entries and exits. I think these differences stem from their experience and account size. I feel more confident now, but as we all know, consistent trading success requires years of experience—at least three years of learning, and yes, blowing up your account (LOL).

The biggest lesson I’ve learned is the importance of cutting losses. There’s no reason to hold on to a losing trade. It’s like when you miss your stop at a train station—you should get off at the next one instead of waiting until the last stop. I hope everyone learns from their own experiences and finds success in the near future.

content:
Just caught back up with the chat.

I'd like to give my thought on some of the things said.

Taking signals is not a long term solution. I can promise you that if you solely rely on signals that you will lose in the long term and let me break it down. A great example of this is yesterday and today. Let's say you took the NVDA trade towards the downside yesterday. Most likely you would have sold on the first push towards the downside because you didn't understand the overall context of the trade. This was a higher timeframe thesis laid out in the pre market prep and we talked about this over the weekend as well. If the market is weak we will be look for NVDA towards the downside. And if you didn't understand this, you would have no conviction to hold for the move towards the downside even though there was a very good chance that it would head lower. 

And today for example lets say you missed the trade yesterday and now you got into NVDA this morning. I mentioned that its a completely different setup and that you have to keep a tight stop on this one as its more aggressive since its close to open. Once again if you didn't understand this it would be hard to capture. Price ended up rejecting off PML and reversing. When it came back up I stopped out quickly because I knew that price was most likely going to reverse. 

What I'm trying to say is that the problem with taking signals is that when you lose you end up taking a full R loss and sometimes even more since you will hold past your stop and when your in a winning trade you sell as soon as your in the green. You can't hold because you don't have conviction for yourself since your relying on someone else but yourself.

And that's just the reality of taking signals. That's why we teach to fish for yourselves. You think Neto became profitable by taking signals. He took some of the concepts that we teach and implemented it to his own trading, where he has his own system, strategy and edge in the markets. 

You saw my statistics for the month of August. Last two weeks of the month weren't the greatest but I ended up making over 29K with a 52% win rate because I had a 1:3.85 RR. My biggest loss was no more than 2K on a single day. When I lose I cut them quick and when I have an A+ setup I win big. 

I think most people understand this that have been in the room for a while but there's always a bunch that don't seem to understand this.

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
content:
Slippage refers to the difference between the expected price of a trade and the actual price at which the trade is executed. This typically happens with market orders, which are executed immediately at the best available price. Since prices can change rapidly, especially in volatile markets or with large orders, the price you get may be slightly worse (or occasionally better) than the price you expected. 

For example, if you place a market order to buy a stock at $100, but by the time your order is executed the price has risen to $101, you experience slippage of $1. Slippage can happen in both buying and selling, and it’s usually more common during times of high volatility or low liquidity.

author: crunchybrewski
content: Most of the tickers we trade in this room have enough volume (contracts switching hands) that the bid-ask spread is pretty tight.  For a lot of my 0 day contracts, the bid ask spread is a few cents and there is enough volume to fill my order before the price moves too far in an unfavorable direction. For instance if I buy a contract for 1$ with the bid at .99 and the ask at 1.01. I can buy and immediately sell the contract for a loss of 2 dollars even without anything else changing because I bought at the ask and sold at the bid. tickers with less volume will likely have much wider spreads and so you can lose money even if the trade didnt move or moved in your direction. Hopefully that adds context to Neto's explanation.

author: ccmclane
content:
Agreed, the way I have heard them described are: 
* Market Order - guaranteed to fill, no guarantee of the price it is filled at
* Limit Order - guaranteed to fill at or better than the price specified if the price is hit, no guarantee of a fill
*  Stop Order - guaranteed to fill at Market once price has traded at or through a specified price (once the price is met, it becomes a Market Order)

**RULES RULES RULES FOR FRIDAY **

If you’re green for the week, only trade with a small **PORTION** of your profits. For example, if you’re up $1,000, risk just $200-$300. Even if you lose it, you’ll still end the week green. 

If you’re green but don’t have enough profits to play with, **DO NOT TRADE**. 

If you’re red for the week, **DO NOT TRADE**. 

Even if you’re green and have profits to spare, you can always take Friday off. Enjoy a 3-day weekend—it’s never a bad idea. 

Remember, Fridays won’t make you, but they can break you. 

Stick to these rules, and you’ll never end the week on a bad note.

content: I traded on my phone when I was a welder at a plant (super fast paced and strenuous) and had some success. I used WeBull because the mobile app is very very good and you can actually get in and out pretty quick. I bought one of those kickstand cases for my phone and I would put it in my welding cabinet where no bosses or anything could see. I kept 1 earbud in and had my sound on and notifications set on my charts for certain levels. Like for example the 5m range established so I'd go ahead and put an alert for above/below those levels by 1 cent. When they broke I'd get alerted, and when they'd come back to retest I'd get another alert! So I'd run over real quick and take my gloves off and get in the trade. Then I'd set an alert 10-15 cents above my stop so I'd get alerted and could stop out if needed. I'd have alerts 5 cents lower than each profit target to give myself time to get to my phone for the pop so I could scale out. I did this for about a year solid. It can be stressful, but once you kind of figure out your little way to do it and whatnot it can be done! Hope this helps man.

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
content:
**RULES RULES RULES FOR FRIDAY**

Seriously, take a screenshot of this and keep it handy. 

**If you’re green for the week**, only trade with a small **PORTION of your profits**. For example, if you’re up $1,000, risk just $200-$300. Even if you lose it, you’ll still end the week green. 

If you’re green but don’t have enough profits to play with, **DO NOT TRADE.**

**If you’re red for the week, DO NOT TRADE.**

Even if you’re green and have profits to spare, you can always take Friday off. Enjoy a 3-day weekend—it’s never a bad idea. 

Remember, **Fridays won’t make you, but they can break you**. 

Stick to these rules, and you’ll never end the week on a bad note.

Hey @everyone,

Just a quick heads-up on why trading options on FOMC days isn’t recommended. The market tends to be super volatile, with quick and unpredictable swings that can throw off even the best setups. It’s often better to wait until the market settles after the announcement, when you can trade with more clarity and less stress. 

Play it safe—there will always be better, more predictable days ahead!

The ongoing union strikes at U.S. ports will most disrupt public companies that rely heavily on international supply chains and the smooth flow of goods through these ports. Some of the most affected industries include:

1. **Retail Companies**:
   - **Walmart (WMT)** and **Amazon (AMZN)**: Both companies are highly dependent on imports for their inventory, particularly goods from Asia. The closure of major ports will lead to delays in restocking and higher transportation costs.
   - **Target (TGT)**: Similar to other large retailers, Target depends on a seamless supply chain to maintain inventory levels and meet customer demand.

2. **Automotive Industry**:
   - **Ford (F)** and **General Motors (GM)**: U.S. automakers rely on a mix of imported parts and components to manufacture vehicles. The Port of Baltimore, the largest importer of cars in the U.S., is one of the ports affected by the strike [oai_citation:3,2024 United States port strike - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_port_strike) [oai_citation:2,US dockworkers' strike paralyzes shipping, threatens economy – DW – 10/01/2024](https://www.dw.com/en/us-dockworkers-strike-paralyzes-shipping-threatens-economy/a-70372925).
   - **Tesla (TSLA)**: Tesla's global supply chain could face disruptions, especially regarding parts and vehicles shipped from overseas factories.

3. **Consumer Electronics**:
   - **Apple (AAPL)**: Apple could face significant disruptions, especially for its iPhones and other devices assembled abroad and shipped via U.S. ports.
   - **Sony (SONY)**: Electronics manufacturers like Sony depend on ports to import components and finished goods, which may see delays.

4. **Food and Beverage Companies**:
   - **Chiquita Brands International**: The Port of Wilmington, a major hub for banana imports, is affected, leading to disruptions in the supply of bananas and other perishable goods.
   - **Tyson Foods (TSN)**: Food producers that rely on imports of raw materials or exports of finished goods may see delays, especially for perishable items [oai_citation:1,2024 United States port strike - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_port_strike).

5. **Apparel Companies**:
   - **Nike (NKE)** and **Gap Inc. (GPS)**: Both companies rely on imported apparel and footwear, and delays at ports will likely disrupt inventory flows and raise costs.

The longer the strike continues, the more severe the impact will be on these companies, which may result in increased costs, inventory shortages, and potential price hikes.

content:
Maybe you should rethink your PT not stop loss. With 1000$ most probably you shouldn't trade with more than 1 con, with risk 30$ it's already 3% of the account, you don't wanna risk more.

author: Bhavika
content: When buying contracts, move the decimal to the right to get the price. So if a contract is 1.25 then one contract is $125. And if you want to lose no more than $50 then the lowest you can sell the contract for is 0.75. Obviously the math changes the more contracts you buy. Also, buying contracts close to or in the money (the contract strike price is close to the stocks current price) for expensive stock like Netflix can be hundreds of dollars. And so if you have a small account, you may need to buy contracts that are more out of the money so that they are cheaper. These may not move as much as ones closer to the money do tho.

**RULES RULES RULES FOR FRIDAY**

Seriously, take a screenshot of this and keep it handy. 

**If you’re green for the week**, only trade with a small **PORTION of your profits**. For example, if you’re up $1,000, risk just $200-$300. Even if you lose it, you’ll still end the week green. 

If you’re green but don’t have enough profits to play with, **DO NOT TRADE.**

**If you’re red for the week, DO NOT TRADE.**

Even if you’re green and have profits to spare, you can always take Friday off. Enjoy a 3-day weekend—it’s never a bad idea. 

Remember, **Fridays won’t make you, but they can break you**. 

Stick to these rules, and you’ll never end the week on a bad note.

author: demchy19
content:
Hi Lauren,
I'm not a professional trader yet; I'm still learning, but I'll share my thoughts on your question. I don't think this follows the 84% rule. If I understand correctly, the 84% rule applies when you have a plan for entering a stock at a specific key level (e.g., the 5-minute opening candle print), and the stock tries to retest that level but fails and goes lower. The 84% rule comes into play when the stock returns to that key level and breaks through it. At this point, you just watch the price reaction at that level. Typically, with the 84% rule, the stock doesn't retest the key level—it just breaks through and moves in the right direction.
From the picture below, we can see that the stock has retested the same level twice. This can give you a stronger confirmation that the level is well established and could push the stock lower. There are likely many sellers above this level, preventing the stock from going higher, so there's a good chance it will drop. But based on your take profit and stop loss, you seem to be in a good position.

author: demchy19
content: Today, I was trading NVDA and followed the 84% rule. I planned to enter on the 1-minute OB, but it didn’t hold; instead, it went through. Once the stock reclaimed that level, it was a good entry point. I entered the trade, but I think I was a bit too quick and didn’t wait for the proper timing. Fortunately, the trade moved in the right direction.

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
content:
**RULES RULES RULES FOR FRIDAY**

Seriously, take a screenshot of this and keep it handy. 

**If you’re green for the week**, only trade with a small **PORTION of your profits**. For example, if you’re up $1,000, risk just $200-$300. Even if you lose it, you’ll still end the week green. 

If you’re green but don’t have enough profits to play with, **DO NOT TRADE.**

**If you’re red for the week, DO NOT TRADE.**

Even if you’re green and have profits to spare, you can always take Friday off. Enjoy a 3-day weekend—it’s never a bad idea. 

Remember, **Fridays won’t make you, but they can break you**. 

Stick to these rules, and you’ll never end the week on a bad note.

**RULES RULES RULES FOR FRIDAY**

If you’re green but don’t have enough profits to play with, **DO NOT TRADE.**

**If you’re red for the week, DO NOT TRADE.**

Even if you’re green and have profits to spare, you can always take Friday off. Enjoy a 3-day weekend—it’s never a bad idea.

author: chunky_beast
content:
<@584423632802021376> I’ll keep this as simple as possible, but please what I’m about to say isn’t meant to be gospel. I don’t like leaving questions unanswered if I can help it. 

When you look at the upcoming earnings you obviously expect an uptick in options trading into that particular week volume wise but what will almost always increase is options holders/open interest (OI) into those options. Using AAPL for example we have a large disparity between Call holders vs Put holders for Nov 1 Weekly’s so with this we can estimate that, as of Friday, the market is currently expecting bullish move into earnings. Plus as you get from Earnings Whispers, on the wider options there was a large volume of Feb 21 265C bought on Friday indicating some bull expects a move towards the upside in the longer term worth putting up $12M. With all this you can infer the market a bullish outlook on AAPL. 

A different case is GOOGL where we can see, as of Friday, there isn’t really any high expectations for explosive short term moves based on next weeks options OI. 

There are other equities you can look at with extremely high bullish option sentiment like AMZN and AMD. 

However this is just a gauge, not a crystal ball. Do your own research and ensure that this correlates with your strategy and playbook. Also if you’re gonna trade shorter dated options into earnings this isn’t a swing where you may lose 60-70%. You can easily lose your equity so you have to be comfortable with a 100% risk to capital overnight.

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
content:
**RULES RULES RULES FOR FRIDAY**

Seriously, take a screenshot of this and keep it handy. 

**If you’re green for the week**, only trade with a small **PORTION of your profits**. For example, if you’re up $1,000, risk just $200-$300. Even if you lose it, you’ll still end the week green. 

If you’re green but don’t have enough profits to play with, **DO NOT TRADE.**

**If you’re red for the week, DO NOT TRADE.**

Even if you’re green and have profits to spare, you can always take Friday off. Enjoy a 3-day weekend—it’s never a bad idea. 

Remember, **__Fridays won’t make you, but they can break you__**. 

Stick to these rules, and you’ll never end the week on a bad note.

author: Jdub
content:
Its not really about being upset because as a human you are going to have emotions. It's all about what you do with those emotions. Am I upset when I take a bigger loss than expected. Of course but its all about how you respond and what you do after the fact. 

Trading is all a game about probabilities. I had conviction coming into this morning on TSLA for a continuation higher and guess what it didn't work out. I wanted to only risk around $2000 on this trade and ended up losing over $4000. But what happened next, I didn't do anything irrational or went to do something dumb. What I did was wait for another opportunity to setup. 

We ended up getting in SPY/ES which was a solid setup and is still working out as I type this out. 

As for relying on trading as income I didn't do this for the longest time. When I started out and even when I was profitable I was still delivering packages on the side. I would next recommend someone to do this full time without some sort of income coming in. Having to "rely" on trading is going to make it very difficult no matter who you are. 

Hope that makes some more sense.

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
content:
**RULES RULES RULES FOR FRIDAY**

Seriously, take a screenshot of this and keep it handy. 

**If you’re green for the week**, only trade with a small **PORTION of your profits**. For example, if you’re up $1,000, risk just $200-$300. Even if you lose it, you’ll still end the week green. 

If you’re green but don’t have enough profits to play with, **DO NOT TRADE.**

**If you’re red for the week, DO NOT TRADE.**

Even if you’re green and have profits to spare, you can always take Friday off. Enjoy a 3-day weekend—it’s never a bad idea. 

Remember, **__Fridays won’t make you, but they can break you__**. 

Stick to these rules, and you’ll never end the week on a bad note.

@everyone <@&1219020123218645102>

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
content:
**RULES RULES RULES FOR FRIDAY**

Seriously, take a screenshot of this and keep it handy. 

**If you’re green for the week**, only trade with a small **PORTION of your profits**. For example, if you’re up $1,000, risk just $200-$300. Even if you lose it, you’ll still end the week green. 

If you’re green but don’t have enough profits to play with, **DO NOT TRADE.**

**If you’re red for the week, DO NOT TRADE.**

Even if you’re green and have profits to spare, you can always take Friday off. Enjoy a 3-day weekend—it’s never a bad idea. 

Remember, **__Fridays won’t make you, but they can break you__**. 

Stick to these rules, and you’ll never end the week on a bad note.

author: Mike Y
content: I've been studying and reading my MM5 notes and a piece that I wrote from Jdub word for word (I write this so not only myself but for many to connect with) :  Higher Time Frame Thesis: If your so fixated on lower time frame 1 min chart and you always sell on pops and take profits, sure you might make $400-$500 on 1 min time frame, but when HTF trade comes you've always sold on its pop. So when you are in a HTF trade you can not hold for HTF move. You can't take higher profits because you always come in as a scalpers mentality and sell on pops.  If you focus on HTF you will be able to capture more of the move.  But since you have a 1" lower time frame trading mentality-you will never capture higher time frame PROFITS!     I hope this connects as I am totally guilty of this!  Granted if $400 or $500 is all you want, I get it, but we as traders are not here to be limited.  to be restricted, to be reckless of trade by fear.  We are here to Capture, to provide and broaden our discovery to trading.  We can do this and we got this!! Just give it time and be patient!

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
content:
**RULES RULES RULES FOR FRIDAY**

Seriously, take a screenshot of this and keep it handy. 

**If you’re green for the week**, only trade with a small **PORTION of your profits**. For example, if you’re up $1,000, risk just $200-$300. Even if you lose it, you’ll still end the week green. 

If you’re green but don’t have enough profits to play with, **DO NOT TRADE.**

**If you’re red for the week, DO NOT TRADE.**

Even if you’re green and have profits to spare, you can always take Friday off. Enjoy a 3-day weekend—it’s never a bad idea. 

Remember, **__Fridays won’t make you, but they can break you__**. 

Stick to these rules, and you’ll never end the week on a bad note.

Hi Team,

author: Reeba
content: Are you guys able to give me some tips on swing trades? How do you not lose sleep by holding trades overnight 😭 what if they don't go your way and how long do you guys keep contracts for? 1 weeks or more?

author: Angel (az)
content:
I can't speak for the pros, but here is my personal experience as a beginner - I'm able to hold the trade and not care because I am comfortable with the risk im exposed to at 2 cons total, I am comfortable with it dropping 50% in value overnight in the worst case. And 2 is easier to manage than 1 IMHO. I don't know how you're sizing but it needs to be what you personally are comfortable with mentally at this point in your journey. I am strict with scaling out at the first pop up which gives you realised gains and it's like a cheat code that makes it easier for you psychologically to hold the second one. The Tesla trade this week for example, my first con scale was 300+ realised, so now psychologically, i am okay with my second con going to -300. (I would not wait that long to stop out, but it lets you breathe and gives you a lot of room mentally). Ever since then, I literally try to not even look at the value of my second con or the price, I am just waiting for the HTF target to hit or structure to break. 

If the trade doesn't work: I believe Jack or Tony said you have your stop losses as usual in terms of trades not going your way, but you have to be more comfortable with a larger percentage drawdown. Stop loss is at where key HTF levels and structures are broken

author: Angel (az)
content: But in reality, I do lose sleep on swing trades because I'm overseas and have to somewhat monitor the swings during market day  🤣

author: demchy19
content:
Usually, red folder news affects the overall market rather than a specific stock. There’s always a possibility that the news will be good, causing the market to go higher, which would also take TSLA higher. On the other hand, if the news is bad, it could bring the entire market down, including TSLA. And sometimes, the news might not affect the market at all.

I’d say trading based on news is a bit like gambling—it’s always a 50/50 chance whether it goes in your direction or against it. Hopefully, that makes sense! 🙂

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
content:
**__RULES RULES RULES FOR FRIDAY__**

Listen up, because this is crucial. Take a screenshot of this and pin it somewhere visible.

**If you're in the green for the week**, only gamble with a tiny slice of your gains. Say you're up $1,000, then play with just $200-$300. Even if you blow it, you'll still walk away with a profit for the week.

If you're green but your profits are too slim to play with, **DO NOT TRADE.**

**If you're in the red for the week, DO NOT TRADE.**

And even if you're sitting pretty with some profits to burn, consider taking Friday off. An extra day to relax isn't something to sneeze at.

Remember, **__Fridays won’t make you, but they can break you. __**

Follow these rules, and you'll never end the week wishing you hadn't played.

author: Lauren (lakatrades)
content:
I hope  you guys are  doing well. I wanted to take a moment to acknowledge that trading comes with its challenges, and today might have been a tough learning curve for some of us, with losses in either profit or dollar value.

I can’t stress enough the importance of implementing stop-loss tools in your trading strategy. This step is crucial for managing risk effectively, especially when dealing with options contracts.

Here’s a quick guide to setting up a stop-loss:
Webull:
1. Go to your position and select Sell.
2. Choose Stop Loss or Stop-Limit Order as the order type.
3. Enter the stop price and confirm the order.


Thinkorswim (TOS):
1. Right-click your position in the Monitor tab and select Create Closing Order > Sell.
2. Set the order type to Stop or Stop Limit.
3. Enter the stop price and review before activating the order.

Please ensure these tools are part of your trading plan to mitigate risks. Also, remember to stick to your strategy consistency and discipline are key to long-term success.

author: Lauren (lakatrades)
content:
Great question! Yes, I prepare a thesis every night based on higher timeframe trends (daily/4H) and intraday setups (15-min/5-min). I identify key levels, plan potential scenarios for both bullish and bearish moves, and focus on reacting to price action rather than predicting.

For your challenge, here are some tips:

Focus on the Bigger Picture: Higher timeframe trends often guide overall bias. Intraday bearish moves might just be pullbacks.
Look for Reversal Confirmation: Don’t assume quick reversals. Wait for signs like volume shifts, candlestick patterns, or break-and-retest setups.
Separate Contexts: Use the higher timeframe for bias and intraday charts for precise entries. Adjust your stop-loss and targets accordingly.
Review Your Trades: Journaling can help spot patterns and refine your ability to switch between timeframes.

content: For example, I developed a new thesis plan today during trading based on the criteria mentioned above.

author: Lauren (lakatrades)
content:
Volume Analysis:

Check if the volume is increasing or decreasing. Rising volume often confirms strong momentum (Option A), while declining volume may indicate consolidation (Option B).
Key Levels:

Observe support and resistance levels (e.g., ORH, YDL). A bounce or rejection at these levels can suggest the next direction.
Relative Strength Index (RSI):

Use RSI to gauge if the stock is overbought or oversold. Overbought signals may lead to consolidation or reversal (Option B).
Candlestick Patterns:

Watch for reversal patterns like dojis or engulfing candles near key levels for a potential consolidation or reversal.
Trend Continuation Signals:

Look for lower highs and lower lows in a downtrend for continuation (Option A).
Market Context:

Consider broader market conditions and sector performance for confirmation of trend continuation or pause.

author: Lauren (lakatrades)
content:
Practical Use of Indicators
VWAP (Volume Weighted Average Price):
Tracks the average price based on volume and price action.

General guideline:
Buy calls above VWAP.
Buy puts below VWAP.

Helps determine whether the price is overextended or needs a pullback.
EMA9 and EMA21 (Exponential Moving Averages):

EMA9 is for short-term trends, while EMA21 represents medium-term trends.
Commonly used for pullback entries in trending markets, especially on the 5-minute chart.
Pullbacks to these levels often coincide with key support, resistance, or liquidity levels.

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
content:
Great second question! 
We typically align our trades with the macro narrative. For example, if the daily/1-hour/15-minute charts are all showing bullish signals, we're looking to enter on a smaller timeframe with a bullish bias. **That's what we consider an A+ setup - when all these timeframes align.** So, we usually aim for the high of the opening range when we're bullish and the low of the opening range when we're bearish. 

However, there can be scenarios where you might see a rejection at the Opening Range High or a bounce off the Opening Range Low, but these would generally need additional confirmation from the broader market context to be considered viable trades. 
Also, we always keep an eye on all relevant key levels like old highs and lows, pre-market levels, and previous day levels, looking for a retest on those levels and waiting for the retest and the eventual reaction. 

Keep an eye on the macro trends to guide your decisions! The trend is your friend!

author: DWC2016
content:
Yea makes sense 100%. But risk and position size are not the same thing and often confused. 

Like Tony will have a position size of $30k but only risk $4k if the trade goes bad which would be %4 risk if the account if it’s a $100k account but if the trade works that how you get those $50k+ days while only risk a small amount. 

Or Ex : You can put on a trade that’s $1000 in size but only actually risk $100-$200 as the stop loss. I think a lot of people get confused between the position size and the stop loss which is the actual risk in the trade. Hope that makes sense. I was confused by this when starting as well 🙏

author: Pierogi
content: Thank you for this. I’m embarrassed to say but I still don’t understand how to set a stop loss at IBKR. I want to have a stop loss at -20%.

author: DWC2016
content:
Yea no problem I think this is a common missunderstanding. I traded crypto for about 6 years so about 80% of the concepts transfer over. 

But yea its a balancing act of the position sizing so you can make money when things works and the actual risk (stop loss) your willing to loss. The stop is the actual risk not the sizing unless you dont follow your stop loss rules then you will doom yourself 😅.

But In futures its a bit more straight forward to set a 20% SL but in options you have to do a bit of math. 

but you have to look at where your stop is and relative to the price of the contract cost if the underlying assest moves xyz percentage then the contract to move roughly the same. These is a video on youtube that explain these things. search " how to set a stop loss based on the underlying asset price" on youtube. 

Also if you type on youtube "how to set a stop loss with IBKR" you should see a few videos that show you. Its fairly simple.

author: demchy19
content:
For me, the EMA 9 and EMA 21 serve as confirmations to stay in a trade longer. These moving averages help identify whether the stock wants to continue in its current trend or if it’s about to reverse. Most of the time, if the stock wants to go higher or lower, it tends to hold either the EMA 9 or EMA 21.

If the stock breaks below (or above) these levels, it can indicate a potential reversal or a larger pullback. At that point, you can decide whether to close the trade or hold it, depending on your strategy.

author: demchy19
content: But again, sometimes EMAs are not that useful if you want to trade using higher timeframes. For example, <@1121621751764369501>  today traded NVDA, if I’m not mistaken. Based on EMA 9 and 21, the stock didn’t hold properly. It looked better on the 5-minute chart, but it still broke below. However, in her case, she used higher timeframes, the VWAP, and also the 5-minute opening range as extra confirmation

author: demchy19
content: So it really depends on the situation and strategy you use

author: Mk
content:
My absolute biggest blunder of a problem is that I do not wait for confirmation. My trade ideas are correct and have learned much from Tony and Jack. But a large part in my trading stems from having the lowest risk possible so I end up trying to catch the bottom for long positions without waiting for confirmation.  Today I had a $1,400 loss on TSLA because I stopped out too early. I re took it later and made $1,600 on it.  Green but could of avoided unnecessary draw down.

My question is, what type of confirmations do you guys look for on trending days? Green 5 min candle close above the level with strong volume or something else?  <@1014389514141184074> <@1121621751764369501> <@792532341565554728>

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
content:
For this setup to work best, there are some essential components:

Break of the level – Price needs to decisively break above or below the identified support or resistance.
Displacement – There should be a noticeable and strong move away from the level after the break. This ensures momentum and liquidity have shifted.
Retest – Price then retraces to retest the broken level.
Reaction – Finally, observe how price reacts during the retest. Strong rejection or confirmation signals the continuation of the move, offering a potential entry point.

Waiting for all these steps helps filter out false breakouts and increases the probability of a successful trade.

author: Mk
content: Thanks for the reply <@1014389514141184074> . I'm with you on all of that... i wait for all of that to recognize the move I want to get into. The MOST critical aspect of this is the last part, the "reaction". Green hammer candle is the most obvious for confirmtion of entry, but this is where I am struggling. I often find myself getting in too early. or too late. If I wait for strong body closure off the retest of the level, then I've missed my entry and stop is too far.. know what I mean?

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
content:
Color of the candle doesn’t have any relevance… you’re looking for reaction on level and Price Action
A red color candle can have a good bullish price action and a green candle can have a good bearish price action

author: Lauren (lakatrades)
content:
If you're a new trader or still working towards consistent daily trades, I strongly recommend starting with just 1-2 contracts to protect your capital. Focus on developing your own daily trading edge and strategy, as this is essential for long-term success.

Copying someone else’s trades might provide short-term results, but it’s not a sustainable approach. Instead, take the time to build your own foundation and confidence in your trading.

Additionally, PLEASE take the time to review the WHOP Accelerator Program and Tony/Jack's videos. They provide invaluable insights and teach you the essential steps needed to succeed in trading.

Make sure to identify the strategy that fits you best and stick with it. Remember, not everyone uses the same strategy, and trying to follow someone else’s approach may lead to confusion. Stay focused and committed to your personal trading journey!

author: Lauren (lakatrades)
content:
Validate Trendline: Ensure it connects two or more significant swing lows/highs without cutting through candles. Retests confirm validity.
Trendline Break: Redraw if price closes decisively beyond the trendline with strong momentum or volume.
New Structures: Adjust for new formations, like flags or consolidations, as they develop.
Confluence Levels: Prioritize trendlines that align with key support, resistance, or Fibonacci levels.
Timeframe Matters: Short-term trendlines (1-min, 5-min) may require frequent adjustments due to volatility.
Price Behavior: Watch for tight consolidation or "riding" along the trendline as a signal for potential breakout.
Stay Flexible: Update trendlines dynamically based on real-time market changes and dominant structures.

author: Nines
content: This is essentially how you counter trend. Say your in a bearish market and you want to take a short but the next bearish key level is a bit far away and you dont wanna short at the current price because its over sold. You wait for order flow to switch from bearish to bullish on the 1h and 4h and then you take a long until that key level is met. Its crucial that you let a bottom form first and not just try and catch the bottom. Never ever try and predict the bottom u let it form and then play the counter trend

Headlines on bloomberg article regarding DeepSeek and AI market. 

“DeepSeek, a Chinese AI startup that’s just over a year old, has stirred awe and consternation in Silicon Valley after demonstrating breakthrough artificial intelligence models that offer comparable performance to the world’s best chatbots at seemingly a fraction of the cost. 

DeepSeek’s emergence may offer a counterpoint to the widespread belief that the future of AI will require ever-increasing amounts of power and energy to develop. 

The app distinguishes itself from other chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT by articulating its reasoning before delivering a response to a prompt. The company claims its R1 release offers performance on par with OpenAI’s latest and has granted license for individuals interested in developing chatbots using the technology to build on it. 

Though not fully detailed by the company, the cost of training and developing DeepSeek’s models appears to be only a fraction of what’s required for OpenAI or Meta Platforms Inc.’s best products. The much better efficiency of the model puts into question the need for vast expenditures of capital to acquire the latest and most powerful AI accelerators from the likes of Nvidia Corp. That also amplifies attention on US export curbs of such advanced semiconductors to China — which were intended to prevent a breakthrough of the sort that DeepSeek appears to represent.”

content: Yesterday, Teslas IV was extremely high. If it moved a couple cents, I was either losing or making $20 or so. So imagine it move very very little, and I lost $100 almost instantaneously. author: Humantorch
content: what's the decision making when taking strike prices in a typical BnR setup? Say we're in 5 BnR and we want to enter at stock price of 118$. There is Strike Price of 119 or up, say 120, 121. What's the recommended way to approach this?

author: StevenP
content: the 119 is 1 otm since stock price is 118. 1 otm strikes are a good balance for day traders to take. usually they have a good delta and the cost is decent. so it makes for good profit compared to cost. if you look at 2 otm sometimes the volume and open interest paired with your thesis on thinking the stock will go to $120 from 118 can be more profitable with a strong move towards the strike price. its really all about your risk and thesis on where the stock will go

I'm not sure if I’d ever want to do something like getting my hearing back I come from a fifth-generation Deaf family, and we’re doing just fine as we are. We can use apps like Ava or Otter for text-to-voice/voice-to-text, but sometimes hearing people just don’t have the patience to wait for a Deaf person to type and respond. 🤷‍♀️

I have two CODA brothers (Children of Deaf Adults) who are both hearing and fluent in American Sign Language. They can easily navigate both world

content:
Hey Traders,
@everyone
Another solid session in the books with our coach JDub! Here’s what we covered today:

🔥 Weekly Trades Recap
Reviewed key setups and how they were executed.

📌 Entry Models
Conservative
Most Conservative
Aggressive

⏳ Timeframes & Execution
Thesis is built on 15’ charts to identify key levels.
Entries are executed on the 1’ chart for precision.

📍 Drawing Levels
Levels are drawn on the 15’ timeframe to track price action.
Targets are adjusted based on liquidity levels.

📰 JDub’s Pre-Market Prep
1️⃣ News Analysis – Understanding market-moving events.
2️⃣ HTF Market Context – Evaluating trends on higher timeframes.
3️⃣ A+ Setups Identification – Looking for high-probability setups based on:
PDH BNR (Previous Day High Break and Retest)
PDL BNR (Previous Day Low Break and Retest)
OR BNR (Opening Range Break and Retest)

📈 Risk & Position Management
Jack’s risk plan – How he manages trades on 1’ and 5’ timeframes.
Sizing Decisions – Adjusting position sizes for different trade setups.
"Look Left" Strategy – Define targets based on liquidity levels.

📊 How to Scale Out of a Trade
Scaling out in stages helps lock in profits while letting winners run. Here’s the approach (with an example, but you can set your own scaling plan):
1️⃣ First Exit – Secure Partial Profits (25%)
Sell 25% at the first key level to lock in profits.
2️⃣ Second Exit – Reduce Risk (25%)
Sell another 25% as price moves further in your favor.
3️⃣ Third Exit – Maximize Gains (25%)
Sell 25% when price hits a major breakout level or extension target.
4️⃣ Final Exit – Let the Runner Go (25%)
Let the rest run using the bar by bar method (trail stop with each new bar on the 1’ timeframe).

Thanks for joining! These sessions are packed with actionable insights—keep showing up, refining your skills, and taking advantage of these learning opportunities.

📅 See you next time! 🚀

Copy of the email which I rec'd from Tony - 

If you’re reading this email, you've already experienced our Accelerator and may have some idea about Traders Lab.

However, I want to take a step back and give you a clear overview of what we’ve built and who this is for.

​

The mission of Traders Lab is to help traders optimize their performance to build a profitable career through tailored education.

Anyone that’s been able to become a profitable trader for a consistent period, it took them at least a few years to get everything right.

Our goal is to cut down those years of trials and tribulations.

​

We spent the last year building Traders Lab to ensure it perfectly supports every trader’s journey, regardless of their experience level.

Whether you’re starting out or are somewhere in that messy middle phase of your trading this is for you.

​

Here’s a breakdown of the three main pillars of Traders Lab:

Curriculum: Our playbooks are the most in-depth trading resources we’ve ever created.
​
Each playbook is meticulously designed with step-by-step modules, detailed examples, and proven best practices to ensure you’re learning the right way from day one.
​
Tailored: We understand that every trader has unique goals, experience levels, and learning styles.
​
That’s why our platform adapts to your specific needs, providing personalized learning paths and targeted resources.
​
Community: The ecosystem is at the heart of what makes Traders Lab special.
​
We’ve created an environment where both beginners and experienced traders can network, share insights, and grow together.

​

And that’s just the tip of the iceberg…

There’s so much more inside Traders Lab that I can’t fit into one email but will share more over the next couple of weeks.

​

Now, anyone can just say all of the above, but actually putting it to work is what drives us.

And, I want to show you just one example of what Traders Lab can do for you.

Here’s one of our top members Paul, who has been able to transform almost every aspect in his trading since joining Traders Lab.

Take a look at his recent message inside our community:


​

We've kept Traders Lab discrete and only available to a limited number of people.

We haven't let anyone from the public join us - that's how much we're prioritizing quality in this program.

Since you've experienced our Accelerator I wanted to extend you the opportunity to potentially join Traders Lab if it's a good fit.

All you have to do is a book a call with our team, if Traders Lab is a fit for your needs we'll offer you the opportunity to join us.

author: Lauren (lakatrades)
content:
To gauge QQQ's relative strength/weakness, compare it to:

📌 SPY (S&P 500) → If QQQ outperforms, tech is strong. If it lags, tech is weak.
📌 IWM (Russell 2000) → Strong QQQ vs. IWM = large caps favored. Weak QQQ = shift to small caps.
📌 QQQ/SPY Ratio → Rising = QQQ stronger, Falling = weaker.
📌 Bond Yields → High yields = QQQ weak, Low yields = QQQ strong.
📌 Volume & Breadth → Strong volume = real strength, Weak volume = possible fake move.

Hope that helps!

content: joined only 1 week ago... Copying them straight up has given me winners and losers.... but you have to handle your own risk/sizing/etc.  Try to make it about the process and evolving away from copying T and J to following along to learn the decision making and flow... easier said than done...  improve scanning technique on multiple symbols and id'ing the key levels with them....  study their pre-market strategy and real-time thought processes and adjustments... it's game changing for me...  seeing them in action helps me modulate my trading frequency and build a better eye for hitting better trades. content: What is your win rate on backtesting and what is your TP target when backtesting, are you just looking for 2:1? I'll be honest, when I first backtested, I had 40% win rate which was fine but could never quite get to 2:1 in my testing. So i kinda trusted the win rate and then learned the scaling correctly in real time because there'a a lot more contextual stuff, market conditions, higher time frames. If your win rate is okay and your ratio is not quite 2:1, then a lot of it might have to do with how you are taking profit as well.

author: DarthTrader
content: I base it off the underlying technical level. I do the math on how much I want to risk per contract and take it accordingly. I actually scale into my position so my initial position isn't huge and my losses are smaller as most trades fail in the first few min if they don't go right away. Once the make a new high or low, I actually add to my position (full) then adjust SL as needed. By this time usually we are breaking the highs/low and retesting. If that fails then break even it is. If not we are good.

author: 𝕁𝕒𝕪
content:
Bro, you lost $30k over 5 years. That’s $6k a year. $500’a month. $125 a week. $75 a day.  

Look at it as your 5 year tuition to learn practice and perfect.  

Are you trading to earn a living. Is it a hobby or are you trading solely to get your losses back ? 

Figure out why you’re trading. You can’t make up 5 years in 1 day or 1 week.  Has it been done in a week or a month SURE. But if we get stuck in a mindset we know is wrong yet are only aware of it after we go against it then the losses are gone and there was no tuition. It was essentially gambling.  

I been there, believe me. I’ve blown $35k in less than 2 months.  I feel your pain. A lot of us do.  

If you make $75 a day and shut her down you will get your losses back in time.  
You’re going to have good days and bad obviously but if your RM is there and you’re actually journaling and going over your journal weekly at least it’s going to make it.  

Anyone can make a trade, we have to find trades.  
All Love Bro. Hope you’re able to get a handle on it all and breathe.

author: Nines
content:
some food for thought for you guys; 

scaling out or taking partials are for those who dont trade the bigger picture. reason u never see me scaling out a contract and holding to my tp because it skews my RR significantly. instead of making 6R ill make only 2.5R or lower. then you wonder why your losses are as big as your winners or even bigger. 

with option its tricker because you almost have to scale out because greeks will kill you if you dont, but if you trade futures or forex i recommend you hold to your tp because the days you lose which you will, it wont hurt because your constantly catching 5R trades on the regular. 

im not saying this to bash on anyone who scales out if that works for you and you have success doing that then keep doing it but for me in my experiene i used to see my losers were as big as my winners even tho i was catching 6R trades but when i would scale out at hod or a random level i had marked it skewed with my RR

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
content:
When Walmart WMT releases its earnings, it often includes commentary from executives about consumer behavior—such as shifts in discretionary spending, preferences for value-driven purchases, or e-commerce growth—which can signal broader economic trends. 
Given Walmart's size and competition with companies like Amazon and Target, these insights can influence investor perceptions of those retailers as well, often leading to movements in their stock prices. 
For example, if Walmart reports strong sales and optimistic guidance, it might boost confidence in the retail sector, lifting stocks like Amazon or Target. Conversely, a weak report or cautious outlook could raise concerns about consumer spending, pressuring those stocks.
It's not a separate report, it's inside the ER.

author: Lauren (lakatrades)
content:
<@402084107951144973>  - 

🔍 1-Min Chart (Left Side)
More sensitive / reactive to short-term price movements.

The “Protect Your Asset” trendline on the 1-min chart is drawn tighter and shows earlier signs of reversal.

This chart captured a break of the downtrend earlier, showing bullish momentum forming right after Scale #3.

Best for quick scalps or precise entry/exit signals if you're managing a trade closely.

Shows micro price action and short-term exhaustion or trend shift faster.

⏱️ Use case: Ideal for day traders wanting to lock in profits quickly or protect positions once momentum shifts.


 5-Min Chart (Right Side)
Less sensitive and shows more confirmed structure.

The “Protect Your Asset” trendline here is wider and slower, but gives a stronger trend confirmation.

The trendline broke after Scale #3, confirming a larger shift in trend on a higher timeframe.

Gives more trustworthy signals when looking for bigger moves or validating a trend reversal.

Smoother and filters out noise compared to the 1-min.

⏱️ Use case: Ideal for swing entries, trailing stops, or holding positions longer with more confidence.

author: mattycardarople
content: Is the 1 minute opening range different from the 5minute opening range? I noticed for example on the NVDA trade today it rejected of the 1min opening range low. Not the  5 min opening range low. The first photo is the 1min opening range top and bottom and then the second one is the 5min opening top and bottom.

author: Kam
content:
hey there, while the key levels to take a trade may be different - the qualifying criteria for a break & retest at any level is the same (e.g. clear displacement; strong/weak price action at level, etc). 

using the 1m opening range is usually a more aggressive entry model, so if using the 1m OR we ideally like to look for confluences at that level (orderblocks or an opening play like a gap & go scenario, pre-market level, news, etc). 

Because of the big gap-down today and aggressive continued selling at the open, using a more aggressive entry model on shorts was necessary to try and capture continuation since in most gap-down scenarios we like to look for pops into higher timeframe levels before looking for setups - this generally leads to a higher probability & longer duration trades on the short side.

the best way to get deeper on this to to backtest and log some data to figure out which levels work best for you and on which tickers

also check out Tony's trade review on NVDA today; he goes over why the 1m opening range setup nicely after the gap-down with orderblock & PML confluence

<#1219022089252503632> 

 hope that helps!

author: Kam
content:
hey <@1323448182851637345>, I'm assuming your trade was a BnR off the 5m opening range. a few points to consider: 

1) on higher timeframes we opened up right in the middle of yesterday's range on the ES, so in order to go long or short at an intraday level like the 5m OR, you ideally need stronger evidence of momentum in either direction. Try zooming out to the 15m or 1hr timeframe to see the bigger picture 

2) the amount of displacement is key for the BnR system. In this case there wasn't a strong push or super strong candle close above the level you're using for the retest. Note the upper wicks (a tell for sellers) on the push above the 5m range on the 1m chart

3) if your entry was on the 9:57 candle, it's likely you didn't wait until the candle closed for confirmation that your level was holding. Remember you want to see strong price action at your level in order to enter. 

Will post a couple of links to videos Jack has made recently that may help with building higher timeframe narratives for your trade ideas as well as good entry confirmation signals

author: dylan10100
content: Took a loss tryna revenge trade Tsla today. 45$ loss just tryna make profit after fomo and got chopped around

author: dylan10100
content: Any recommendations?

author: clelaw
content: If you fall into revenge trading that suggests you do not have the control and confidence to take multiple setups in a day. Limit yourself to 1-2 trades a day max. Have a plan going in, and enter only if your plan unfolds. Practice sitting on your hands and doing nothing when your setup is not showing up. You have to trust your expected value and be okay with losing sometimes.

author: dylan10100
content: I’m sorry I should have said this differently. I had fomo and decided to trade when my situation didn’t unfold like you said. I called it revenge but I shouldn’t have since it was my 1 and only trade.

author: clelaw
content: Ah, got you. Yeah that happens sometimes. It still just comes back to sticking to your rules. One of the best pieces of advice I was given was that it is always better to see a trade you wish you were in than to be in a trade you wish you were not. It takes practice to just watch something run and not pull the trigger, but at the end of the day it comes back to your strategy and expected value.

content: Hi. Where can I learn more on IV crush and other factors that can lead to such a loss. I was only doing paper trading today but had a >$1000 loss on 10 MSFT contracts for a relatively smaller pullback.

author: Kash
content: Hi honestly IV (implied volatility) is important, but I do not look at it in form of percentage/numbers. I just undestand it by looking at other factors that indicate to me high IV which is reaction of the price in the market. Usually after a big move (earning, news, big gap up, gap down, market expective a move) in the market the IV will be more juiced up which will cause bigger loss or gain and option prices being expensive. So this morning Jack was looking for the IV to be crushed on msft with a dip, which is in the opposite direction on the reaction of the price.\

author: Kash
content: There is a lot more to it, but I like to keep it simple as I look for reasons to not take a trade all the time. When IV is not right or any factor I do not like I just sit back/

author: BrokeAintNoJoke
content:
Part of the risk with holding overnight and over weekend. A war could breakout, terrorist attack, natural disaster, fraud report, etc. 

Only trade with what you’re willing to lose because overnight is a crapshoot. 

Very unfortunate that Moody released the downgrade. I would even guess it was strategically timed as the market has rebounded from earlier lows. We just have to accept it as part of the game. 

Once you have a proven system to trade and confidence from back and forward testing, it is easier to accept the market for what it is, uncertain. 

Your edge in uncertainty is your back and forward tested system with proven probable edge and sound risk management. 

You have to know if we go to war overnight you’re okay with losing whatever is in the market overnight. 

I have lost quite a bit from following alerts and it has made me a better trader.

author: Jose96
content: Maybe you’re not sizing up and down correctly based on your stoploss. Usually your SL should be somewhere in the chart that invalidates your trade thesis. Based on your entry, you will sometimes have 20-30cents stoploss, and sometimes 1-1.5dollars. If you want to keep your losses the same, you shouldn’t size the same when your SL is 30cents vs when it is 1 dollar. For example if you are okay losing around 100$ per trade and aiming for at least 200$profit, for a 20cent SL, you could buy 10 contracts (assuming 50dollars per 1dollar move of the underlying, 0.2x50x10cons=100usd), but if your SL is 1dollar you could buy 2contracts to play it safe(assuming the same 50dollar per 1dollar move of the underlying, 1x50x2=100). Both cases, if your stoploss hits you’ll lose around 100$(maybe a little more bcoz how options behave). At least that’s the way i size up to keep my losses small.

author: Jose96
content: What i explained was based on the stock itself, but trading the option contracts. Say a stock is at 200 and based on market structure, the stoploss would be a break below 199.8. If you buy calls when the stock is at 200, your stoploss would be a 20cent move. If you buy 10calls, and you assume every will decrease 50$ per 1dollar move of the stock, a 20cent move will equal approx 100usd loss (0.2$ x 50$ x 10cons = 100). It wont be exact becoz of how contracts work, but should be a decent rule of thumb if you buy 1otm contract(40-50delta). If the SL is at 199, thats a 1dollar move, so if you want to only lose around 100usd if you lose the trade, then you would buy 2contracts (1$ x 50$ x 2cons = 100). If you buy the same 10cons for a 1dollar SL, you could lose around 500usd (1$ x 50$ x 10cons = 500). This is just something i use to sort of know how many contracts i’m okay buying for a specific trade opportunity, hope it helps a little

author: Elvis
content: I spent the day to figure out the options buying power so I hope this helps others as well, the contract price does not mater as buying power it’s the stock price that needs to be used to size. Let’s say a contract delta is .5. Tesla price is 345 and nvidia price is 135. The options will move 50 cents on 1 dollar move in the stock price. So if you have a 1% move on nvidia this would be 1.35 dollars so the contract will move about 67 cents and same 1% move on Tesla will be 3.45 dollars so the contract will move 1.72 dollars. So to get same size and risk consistently buying power needs to be measured by stock price. So if your consistent buying power is $1000 that you always need to buy 1000 worth of stock price not contract price to have consistent buying power. Hope others find it helpful, I spent some time doing options calculus haha. But again this depends on delta and that you are always taking the same contract for example always one out the money.

author: Elvis
content: So the way I do this now is if I buy 2 Tesla contracts, stock price being 345 to be consistent I need to divide the other stock price into Tesla to get a ratio. So for nvidia at 135 I take 345/135=2.55 so for every Tesla contract I need to buy 2.55 nvidia contract to be consistent day over day. And for all others apply the same math

author: GoodVibez
content: At what Price point did you enter your shorts? This is something that I've kept in mind as I've experience a few big hit and have seen some comrades take some massive hits. This one thing... the market is predisposed to go higher. It's nature. We plant seeds so they can grow. Big Institutions want more, not less. So moves down aren't beneficial in the broader picture. I only enter puts in the short-term sense. IF it hits my stop loss or doesn't move towards my target with immediate conviction... I'm out that trade. I also don't leverage as much when entering shorts. Holding shorts for swings is a no-go in my rule book. I wait for big retracements or breakout levels and buy UP for time out. The likelihood your cons recover with longs/calls is higher. So the general consensus...CUT YOUR LOSSES, before the losses become too large for you to recover from. Can't recover if you don't have any funds to recover with. And the longer you wait... the more theta will eat your liquidity.

The key to trading options lies in momentum and volatility volume needs to come in.
If you're trading zero-day options and your stock doesn't move in your favor or just consolidates around  the first 10 to 15 minutes, you're likely to lose premium. Even if the move eventually goes your way, unless it's a big and immediate shift, recovering that lost premium is tough.
The best approach Cut your losses quickly.
Options are tricky. That's why traders like Tony prefer trading during the early market hours your trade usually plays out within 5 minutes. You either win or lose, but you avoid time decay, which is an extra loss that many beginners overlook.

Only consider swing trading if you're truly skilled at reading charts and fully understand market conditions. In today’s market, a single news event can invalidate all your technical levels news plays a major role.

author: Sean
content:
I delt with this alot recently. Slowly starting to over come it, but there are a couple things that come to mind. 

One of the bigger things that helped me was changing my goals. I used to focus on profits and losses. Money. Greed and fomo were getting to me. Especially when seeing others prosper. 

I decided to switch to more process focused goals (i.e. Did i follow my plan, respect my stop, respect my take profits...etc).  Doing so , I think, in time the profits will flow. 

Also realizing that is more about probability.  If you take the same trade/setup every day over a long period of time, you'll win out in the end if you have a proven edge in the market. Backtest & journal. Reflect. Have set max loss per trade and max loss per day, and max amount of trades per day. Implement what helps regulate those emotions in other aspects of your life when you feel them arise. For me, shutting things down and walking away and exercising helps settle things down. 

Hope this helps. 

Don't give up. This is a long drawn out battle against ourselves. Master the mind, master the markets.

content:
Pivot (P) = (High + Low + close) /3 -> (Fair Price derived from Yestarday's Range. Candles closing above Pivot tells us Bullish scenarios & below Pivot tells us Bearish scenarios) Breakout Above Pivot takes to R1, R2.. and breakout below Pivot takes us to S1, S2.. etc) 

R1 = 2P - L
S1 = 2P - H

R2 = P  + (H - L) 
S2 = P - (H - L)

R3 = R1 + (H - L) 
S3 = S1 - (H - L)

author: Bhargav
content:
From $500 to $7,876 – My Journey of Patience, Discipline, and Belief

Hey everyone,

I wanted to take a moment to share something close to my heart – not to boast, but to hopefully inspire anyone who's feeling stuck or uncertain in their trading journey.

I joined this trading community about a year and a half ago. Back then, I was just eager to learn, hungry for growth, and like many of you, figuring things out one step at a time. It wasn’t always smooth. There were days filled with doubt, losses that made me question everything, and moments when I wondered if this journey was really for me.

But I kept showing up.

I studied, practiced, journaled my trades, learned from my mistakes, and leaned on this community for support and accountability. Every win and every loss taught me something valuable – not just about trading, but about myself.

In June, I decided to take on a personal challenge: turn $500 into $5,000. Not only did I hit that milestone, but I ended the challenge with a $7,876 account.

Yes, the numbers are exciting – but what I’m truly proud of is the mindset it took to get there: patience, consistency, emotional control, and unwavering belief.

This journey has shown me that it’s not about overnight success – it’s about persistence, process, and trusting that your time will come if you don't give up.

To anyone in this community who’s still grinding, still learning, still waiting for that breakthrough: keep going. You’re closer than you think.

Much love and gratitude to all of you who've been part of this path. The journey is far from over — let’s keep growing, together. Big Thanks to <@717554586843611217> , <@801169196015943731> and all the Mentors here.

– Bhargav

author: SK
content:
This is awesome and will definitely give it a try. For better understanding, can you help me understand how are the pivot levels being defined/calculated of? 

So you use R1-3, S1-3 as your profit tragets based on the direction of move, right?

author: Brute7
content:
correct! 

Pivot (P) = (H + L + C) / 3

Resistance 1 (R1) = 2 * P − L

Support 1 (S1) = 2 * P − H

Resistance 2 (R2) = P + (H − L)

Support 2 (S2) = P − (H − L)

Resistance 3 (R3) = R1 + (H − L)

Support 3 (S3) = S1 − (H − L)

author: Brute7

Breakthrough through pivot downward (Likely downward trend)

author: Brute7
content:
This was drawn manually before I created the script, and I hope it helps illustrate my experience.

Without R3 marked, many intraday traders might continue holding their positions, expecting further upside. Due to FOMO, they may end up selling only after the price starts dropping. Since I have R1, R2, and R3 plotted, I would sell a few contracts at R1 and the remaining at R2 and R3.

Again, at R1 we saw strong price action, which drove the move all the way to R3 and beyond. This allowed me to re-enter the trade at R1, sell a few contracts at R2, and the rest at R3.

I was able to complete script for ( Intraday Session Levels (Pre-Mkt, 5min, 15min)) and will only publish after testing it tomorrow. 

Quick glance of this indicator. 

Intraday Session Levels: Pre-Mkt, 5m, 15m (Auto-Reset)
Automatically plot the most important live intraday levels for each trading day—no manual work required!

**What this script does:**
**1. Pre-Market High & Low:**
Tracks and draws the live high and low from 4:00 AM to 9:30 AM ET. These are key reference points as regular trading opens.

**2. First 5-Minute Candle High & Low:**
After 9:35 AM ET, automatically draws horizontal rays for the high and low of the opening 5-minute range (9:30–9:35 AM ET).

**3. First 15-Minute Candle High & Low:**
After 9:45 AM ET, draws rays for the high and low of the initial 15 minutes (9:30–9:45 AM ET), used by many for breakout/reversal setups.

**4. Automatic Cleanup:**
All plotted levels are cleared after 4:00 PM ET, so your chart is always clean for the next session.

**5. Fully Automatic, Live Updates:**
The script updates in real time, resets for each new day, and handles all session times in U.S. Eastern Time.

author: MDizzy
content: <@832720687193522227> The S and R levels seem uniformly spaced and not tied to any particular level to the left. Any way for it to "look left" for you maybe finding previous pivots?

author: Brute7
content:
<@739730143693766676> Great question! The S/R levels in this script are classic Floor Pivots, which are always calculated from just the previous regular session’s high, low, and close—not by looking for swing points or historical pivots “to the left.” This makes them uniformly spaced and mathematically derived, not price action-based.

This style is perfect for scalping and intraday trading, because it gives you instantly actionable levels that reflect the market structure from the most recent session—great for gaps, mean reversion, and fast trades at key S/R zones right from the open.

There’s a ton of room to customize

You could script additional pivots using longer historical data (multi-day, multi-week, or even price-action “look left” swing pivots).

You can also add as many custom levels or dynamic pivot algorithms as you want, depending on your strategy.

If you want a “look left” style (true swing or historical pivots), that’s a very different type of script—totally possible, but would need to be designed to scan X bars back for true support/resistance.

This one is focused on consistency, speed, and using “yesterday’s map” for today’s trades.

**However, I like your suggestion and I will release v4.0 version to plot the pivots and S/R levels from the last 10 sessions as well.**
